data.title: GOP lawmakers push back on Hegseth decision to livestream execution
data.description:
Republican lawmakers are pushing back on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decision to livestream the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in Texas in 2009. 

Lawmakers in both chambers said the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families and the public showing of the firing squad is something oppressive dictatorships perform that is beneath America. 

Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has disagreed with Hegseth’s decision to fire former Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, said Friday he supports the sentence of death but livestreaming executions is “what jihadists do. America is better than that.” 

Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) said Friday that the execution, which is set to take place Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at Fort Hood, shouldn’t be a livestreamed “spectacle,” arguing the focus should be on “justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment.” 

“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” Bresnahan said in a post on social media. 

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center in November 2009, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian. He injured 32 others in what was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation. 

Hasan, an American-born Muslim, was heard screaming “Allahu akbar,” or “God is great.” The attack ended when Hasan was shot four times and detained by civilian security officers. He is now paralyzed from the waist down.

Hasan said during his opening statement at the 2013 trial, where he was his own attorney, that the “evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter.” He said he carried out the mass shooting in response to the U.S. wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said Seneca “warned that Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them.” 

“A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” Curtis wrote Friday, adding the planned livestream “risks feeding that appetite.” 

“The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity,” he said. “Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.” 

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who said voting to confirm Hegseth was the “biggest regret” of his political career, said Hasan should face the death penalty, but streaming the execution is “beyond disgusting.” 

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis said late Thursday. “It should not be happening in America.” 

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who did not vote to confirm Hegseth, said there is no need to livestream any execution, arguing she expects such a decision from “terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.” 

“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski said Friday in a post. “How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision.” 

Hegseth’s office declined to comment on the lawmakers’ remarks.

But some Republicans welcomed Hegseth’s decision, which he shared during a Thursday interview with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec. 

Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lauded the Defense secretary’s decision as “excellent.” 

“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” Ogles wrote Friday. “We will be watching.” 

Hegseth has said he wanted the “harshest lawful punishment” for Hasan, saying in September that he asked President Trump for final approval for the execution, which will be the first military execution in more than 60 years. 

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during Thursday’s interview with Posobiec. 

Hasan was found guilty on all 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder by a military jury, which sentenced him to death. The Supreme Court denied his final petition in April last year. 

Vice President Vance was skeptical that the livestream would take place, but he said if it does, he will not be watching. 

“This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” the vice president told reporters in Lima, Ohio. “The people that he was meant to treat, the Army soldiers he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems, he took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived.” 

“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said. “Now that said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

When asked Friday about livestreaming Hasan’s execution, Trump said “we’ll be making a determination on that.” 

But minutes later, when he was asked if he approved the livestream, the president said, “Did I approve? Absolutely.”

It was not clear whether Trump meant that he had approved the execution or the livestreaming.

Unsurprisingly, defense-focused Democrats in both chambers of Congress slammed Hegseth’s decision, arguing once again that he is not fit for the role. 

Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Friday that livestreaming an execution is a “barbaric spectacle” and is another “stunt” by Hegseth to “distract from his tenure’s repeated failings which have only weakened our national security and standing in the world.”

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), another Armed Services panel member who has tussled with Hegseth in the past, called for the Defense secretary’s removal, saying the Trump administration should be “delivering for the American people,” not “glorifying violence.”

“There is no doubt that Nidal Hasan is a murderer who took the lives of 13 people and injured dozens. He should face justice for that. But a public execution? Here in the United States?” Kelly, a former Navy pilot, said on Friday. 

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), a House Armed Services Committee member and former Army paratrooper, said Hasan’s “actions were horrific,” but livestreaming his execution is “not an answer.” 

“A public execution only gives our adversaries fodder for anti-American propaganda that makes us less safe,” Crow, a vocal Hegseth critic, said in a statement Friday. “Pete Hegseth’s self-absorbed hunger for power, attention, and violence is disgusting and beneath the office he holds. He is not fit to lead.”

Army retired three-star Lt. Gen. Sean MacFarland, who was the commander of Fort Hood and approved Hasan’s death sentence, panned the livestream as a “terrible idea,” writing the U.S. “surrenders” a piece of moral high ground in the U.S. military’s campaigns against al Qaeda and ISIS. 

“Once it is aired, it is bound to make it harder for our service members to be seen as ‘the good guys’ in foreign lands. How many insurgents were inspired to attack our troops by photos from Abu Ghraib prison? Worst of all, it will make Nidal Hassan an international martyr,” MacFarland said in a Thursday post on LinkedIn.

data.title: Federal judge: DOJ cannot request states' voter lists for eligibility database
data.description:
A federal judge struck down on Friday the Justice Department’s nationwide effort to collect voter registration records and identify suspected non-U.S. citizens, blocking the Trump administration from continuing the program even in states that voluntarily cooperated.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington ruled the department exceeded its legal authority and violated federal privacy laws by requesting sensitive voter information and sharing it with other agencies to identify people’s citizenship status.

The 78-page ruling struck down the DOJ’s entire voter list maintenance policy, invalidating it nationwide. The decision came after multiple states similarly won challenges against the Justice Departments rule in their respective jurisdictions.

“DOJ cannot run roughshod over longstanding laws that were carefully crafted to protect the rights of American people,” Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, wrote.

The decision stems from an April lawsuit filed by voting rights group Common Cause and four voters, who accused the administration of attempting to create a “sprawling new voter surveillance and purging apparatus” ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The plaintiffs argued the Justice Department was attempting to seize control of voter registration procedures traditionally overseen by states, putting eligible Americans at risk of being wrongfully removed from voter rolls.

The program began last year following an executive order from President Trump directing federal officials to work with states to identify potential election law violations.

The DOJ subsequently requested unredacted voter registration lists nationwide, seeking sensitive information including names, addresses and partial Social Security numbers.

At least 18 states complied, allowing the department to share their voter records with the Department of Homeland Security and check citizenship status through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database.

Participating states also agreed to remove voters identified as ineligible within 45 days of notification.

Sooknanan found the department failed to adequately consider the risk of mistakenly removing eligible voters despite knowing federal citizenship records contained inaccuracies.

The judge cited a 2006 Social Security Administration audit that found approximately 3.3 million U.S. citizens had been misidentified as noncitizens.

“The Court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more,” Sooknanan wrote.

data.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to look at 2016 election lawsuit against Clinton: Report
data.description:
President Trump asked the Supreme Court on Friday to reopen his dismissed lawsuit against former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, reviving claims that she and other political adversaries orchestrated an effort to sabotage his 2016 presidential campaign by tying it to Russia.

Trump filed the appeal after a federal judge dismissed his case and ordered the president, as well as his former attorney, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in sanctions. A federal appeals court upheld both rulings last year.

In Friday’s filing, Trump’s attorneys argued the lower courts improperly punished them for pursuing legitimate legal claims, according to Reuters.

As of late Friday night, the lawsuit appeared on the Supreme Court’s online docket system, but the page did not yet list the reported filing. The most recent document available tied to the legal challenge was a late August application requesting more time to file its appeal, which Justice Clarence Thomas approved, extending the deadline to Friday, Oct. 9.

The attorneys wrote that the decision reflected “a deeply troubling trend of federal courts using sanctions and disciplinary threats to punish the president and his lawyers for legitimate legal positions that those courts (erroneously) reject,” per Reuters.

“The court’s intervention is necessary to protect the presidency, and to prevent judicial disagreement from becoming a license to punish its advocates,” the lawyers continued.

Trump first filed the lawsuit in 2022, accusing Clinton, former FBI Director James Comey, the Democratic National Committee and others of conspiring to undermine his presidential bid by bolstering allegations that his campaign colluded with Russia.

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the case in September of that same year, finding Trump’s claims were legally insufficient and that some were filed too late.

Middlebrooks later sanctioned Trump and Habba, describing the lawsuit as a “two-hundred-page political manifesto” and accusing the president, who was not in office at the time of the challenge, of using the courts to advance his political grievances.

The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal and sanctions in 2025. The unanimous three-judge panel, which included Trump appointee Andrew Brasher, found many of lawsuit’s arguments “frivolous.”

The appeal follows Trump’s recent comments that he could have taken action against Clinton, as well as former Presidents Obama and Biden, but chose not to out of respect for the presidency.

“I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden,” Trump told reporters while discussing the possibility of facing another impeachment should Democrats regain control of Congress.

data.title: Zelensky decries US-Russia diesel deal: 'Gifts to Putin will not bring peace'
data.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky lambasted President Trump’s Friday deal allowing Russia to supply the U.S. and global market with diesel, arguing the move would give the Kremlin more money to fund its war in Ukraine and undermine peace efforts.

“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelensky wrote in a lengthy post on social platform X. “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

Following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel across the globe to mitigate skyrocketing fuel prices tied to both the Ukraine war and the U.S.’s war in Iran.

News of the agreement came as Zelensky’s negotiating team was in Florida for two days of talks with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on a possible ceasefire, including a proposal to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote in a Friday afternoon Truth Social post.

The Treasury Department also issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Zelensky questioned the timing of Trump’s announcement and suggested to reporters that the Ukrainian delegation was being used as a “smokescreen” to cover for the agreement with Russia.

“Our Ukrainian team, our negotiating team, is now in Florida for a two-day visit to hold talks with the American team on ending this terrible war, or at least on securing a ceasefire,” he said in remarks translated into English.

Ukraine’s leader continued, “And at this very moment, while our team is talking with the American team in Florida, at this very moment, the President of the United States is talking with the leader of the Kremlin, the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression.”

The war in Ukraine has waged on for over four years since Russia invaded its westward neighbor in February of 2022. Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Kyiv for the first time in early September to restart peace negotiations between the two countries, which had stalled when the U.S. entered its own military conflict.

Zelensky argued the revenue generated from Russian diesel sales “means more money for this war, more money to inflict suffering on us, without a doubt.“ 

“It only feeds Putin and gives him the ability to fight even more,” he said, describing the agreement as a “weak decision by strong partners.”

Trump, meanwhile, has floated the deal as a way to bring down fuel costs for American farmers, ranchers and truck drivers as energy proxies climb ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Diesel prices averaged $6.28 per gallon as of Friday, compared with $3.68 a year earlier, according to AAA.

data.description:

The Big Story 

GOP priorities alienate MAHA supporters

Supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda are feeling betrayed by the Republican Party as the administration cozies up to industry insiders and lawmakers support legislation contrary to their values. 

© AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin

At last week’s MAHA summit, industry insiders representing artificial intelligence, big business and the pharmaceutical industry were given the stage alongside top Trump administration officials. Less represented at the event were MAHA activists. 

 

Voters in this bloc are characterized by their support for Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as well as distrust of vaccine mandates and chemical and agriculture corporations. 

 

“Do we vote for someone who supports vaccine mandates … or do we vote for someone who is actively supporting pesticides and poison in our foods that our babies and children eat on a daily basis?” said Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America. “It’s an impossible decision, and this is why many of our moms are saying they’re going to stay home, or vote independent, write somebody in.” 

 

MAHA supporters were left disappointed earlier this year when the GOP’s farm bill included provisions to extend the deadline for the EPA to re-review health impacts of pesticides that are already on the market. 

 

For pesticides that were on the market prior to a 2007 update to the law, the deadline had previously been 2026. The farm bill would extend it to 2031. 

 

Jeff Hutt, who worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign, agreed that many of the MAHA supporters who backed Trump in 2024 specifically because of Kennedy may stay home. Republicans shouldn’t count on those votes, he said, because the party is more beholden to Trump than to the MAHA ideals.  

 

“The Republican Party really went from being a big tent party in ‘24 to a pup tent party in ‘26. I think a lot of those voters are going to stay home,” said Hutt.

data.title: Live updates: Trump rallies voters in upstate New York after Putin diesel deal announcement
data.description:
President Trump Later is holding a rally in upstate New York after focusing his crunch-time campaign blitz for GOP candidates in red states.

He’s speaking in Syracuse, N.Y., to give a last-minute boost to Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — whom nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave a 10 percent chance of winning as of Thursday night.

Within the past week, the president has made stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama and Nebraska — all of which he claimed in 2024. This weekend, he’ll be in Tennessee and Alabama, with a rally in Alaska next week.

The visit comes after Trump announced Russia will supply the U.S. and global market with diesel amid soaring fuel prices.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

The president also set in motion an administrative panel Friday to investigate mortgage fraud allegations against Federal Reserve board of governors member Lisa Cook in his latest effort to fire her. The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee, Trump said in a written memo.

Follow live below.

data.title: UAE says Flydubai suspect intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport
data.description:
The Flydubai co-pilot who attacked the plane’s captain with an axe last month intended to crash the aircraft into a passenger terminal at an Israeli airport, according to authorities in the United Arab Emirates.

The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, planned to seize control of the 182-passenger aircraft and crash it into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv to cause mass casualties, the UAE’s top prosecutor said Friday.

In a statement carried by state-run news agency WAM, the official said the assailant carried out the attack “with the intention of causing the greatest possible number of human casualties.”

Authorities said Hammami was inspired by the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the U.S., and had taken two previous flights from Dubai to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route and airport.

The findings shed new light on the Sept. 30 attack, which forced a FlyDubai passenger plane bound for Israel to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent struggle in the cockpit.

The axe-wielding assailant attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot with 17 years of flying experience, as the aircraft traveled over a region near Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

Despite suffering serious injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene as the plane rapidly lost altitude.

The aircraft plunged an estimated 14,000 to 16,000 feet in less than a minute before passengers were able to restrain the attacker and two reserve pilots took control. The plane safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

After receiving treatment from hospitals in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi, Machchhar later described the struggle during a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

“When I was on the ground, I realized that the aircraft is going down,” Machchhar said in Hindi, according to a translation by The Associated Press. “And I told myself, ‘This is the last push, Smit. The door is right there.’”

Modi praised the captain for preventing what he described as another Sept. 11-style attack, saying he showed “the highest form of courage.”

In Friday’s statement, prosecutors said Hammami confessed to acting alone and provided a detailed account of his preparations and motives in the presence of his lawyer.

data.title: Watch live: Trump takes midterm campaign push to deep-blue New York
data.description:
President Trump will take his midterm message to Syracuse, N.Y., on Friday evening, rallying Republicans as the party looks to flip the governor’s mansion and make gains in next month’s elections.

Trump is expected to campaign alongside GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman, who is looking to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in a state where Republicans have struggled to win statewide for decades.

The New York stop is a detour from Trump’s recent swing through red states, where Republicans are scrambling to protect their congressional majorities amid troubling midterm polling.

The president is also expected to make campaign stops in Tennessee, Ohio and Alaska in the coming days. 

The event is scheduled to begin at 7:30 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: Trump sends mixed signals on livestreaming Hasan execution
data.description:
President Trump on Friday seemed undecided on whether the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed like the Pentagon announced.

“Well, they’re making a determination about that, but he will be killed, it will be through firing squad,” Trump told reporters before departing for a rally in Syracuse, N.Y. “He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people and he’s totally nuts.”

“So, I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him,” he continued.

He didn’t answer whether he would watch it. The Pentagon on Thursday said the firing squad execution of Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood, Texas shooter, would be livestreamed on Dec. 3.

It will be the military’s first execution in six decades. The plan to livestream it quickly drew fierce criticism from Republicans and Democrats.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), wrote on the social platform X that he agrees Hasan should face the death penalty, “but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting.”

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” Tillis wrote.

Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed (D-R.I.) said in a statement that Hegseth’s plan is “a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters,” and is “absolutely shameful and damaging to America’s interests and core values.”

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people.

Vice President Vance told reporters Friday in Lima, Ohio that he wouldn’t be watching the livestream.

“I’ve seen those announcements. I don’t know if that’s actually going to happen,” Vance said.

“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” he continued. “Now that said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

data.title: Murkowski on public execution: 'I'd expect this from terrorists and dictators'
data.description:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) on Friday urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood shooter.

“There is no need to livestream any execution, including this one,” Murkowski said on the social platform X. “I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

The Alaska Republican argued that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to broadcast Hasan’s death by firing squad would have immense consequences, including bolstering his fame and fulfilling his wish for martyrdom.

“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” she continued. “How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision.”

Her remarks add to mounting bipartisan criticism of Hegseth’s plan to publicize Hasan’s execution, scheduled for Dec. 3 at Fort Hood in Texas.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted in 2013 of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the military base four years earlier. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death — the first military execution in more than six decades.

During his trial, Hasan reportedly told military mental health workers that he hoped to become a martyr if executed.

Hegseth confirmed Thursday the execution would be open to the public and livestreamed.

“We’ll make sure that the people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he said.

Murkowski joins GOP Sens. John Curtis (Utah) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) in opposing the broadcast.

Tillis called the plan “beyond disgusting,” while Curtis warned that livestreaming the execution risks turning capital punishment into entertainment.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) also condemned the move, and called for Hegseth’s immediate removal on Friday, comparing the planned broadcast to public executions carried out by U.S. adversaries Iran and the Taliban.
